name: EMQX
license: Business Source License 1.1 since 5.9.0 (May 2025; source-available, not OSI open source, each version becomes Apache 2.0 after four years); Apache 2.0 core up to 5.8.x; EMQX Cloud is proprietary
summary: An Erlang MQTT broker built for very large device fleets, with a SQL rule engine, now under the Business Source License.
intro: Devices connect to EMQX over MQTT 5.0, 3.1.1 or 3.1, over WebSockets or MQTT over QUIC, or through gateways for MQTT-SN, CoAP and LwM2M. The broker keeps each client’s session and subscriptions and copies every published message to the matching subscribers. Nodes are Erlang VMs joined by Erlang distribution. Since 5.0, a layer called Mria splits them into core nodes, which hold and replicate the routing table, the topic tree and persistent session data, and replicant nodes, which take client connections and receive changes asynchronously through a replication log. Replicants can be added or removed without growing the full mesh between cores. A built-in rule engine runs SQL such as `SELECT payload.temp FROM "plant/+/temp"` on each message and sends the results to Kafka, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, S3 and more than 50 other systems.

Since 5.9.0 (May 2025) there is one edition under the Business Source License 1.1. It is free for non-production use and for production on a single node, unless you offer it to third parties as a hosted service or embedded in a product; schools and non-profits may use it freely when not for commercial profit. Clusters need a commercial licence (a 15-day trial allows 10,000 sessions). Each version becomes Apache 2.0 four years after release. EMQX Cloud Serverless is free up to 1 million session minutes, 1 GB of traffic and 1 million rule actions a month, then $2.00 per million session minutes, $0.15 per GB and $0.25 per million rule actions, for up to 1,000 connections. Dedicated Flex starts at $234 a month; BYOC and self-managed Enterprise are quoted (list prices checked 6 October 2026).
strengths: Built for scale: EMQ reported 100 million MQTT clients connected to one 23-node cluster when it released 5.0
SQL rule engine inside the broker filters and reshapes messages and writes them to Kafka (both ways), databases and object storage with no extra service
Many ways in: MQTT 5.0, 3.1.1 and 3.1, MQTT over QUIC and WebSockets, and gateways for MQTT-SN, CoAP and LwM2M
Managed options from a free Serverless tier to dedicated clusters and BYOC in your own cloud account; 6.0 added durable, load-balanced message queues on `$q/` topics
limits: No longer open source: since 5.9.0 the BSL allows production use only on a single node, and never as a hosted service or embedded in a product you sell, without a commercial licence
The last Apache 2.0 line is 5.8 (5.8.9, December 2025), and even there connectors such as Kafka were BSL-licensed enterprise code

Serverless caps at 1,000 connections and 1,000 message transactions per second; session minutes include offline clients with persistent sessions, connections under a minute count as a full minute, and traffic is billed in both directions
Dedicated Flex charges its hourly base fee whatever the load, and a suspended pay-as-you-go deployment still costs $0.06 an hour for data retention
Running your own cluster means operating Erlang nodes; core nodes should share a private network with under 10 ms of latency

sections.title: EMQX, HiveMQ and Mosquitto
sections.intro: Three widely used MQTT brokers. All speak MQTT 5.0, so devices can move between them; they differ most in licence and in what you have to pay for to run more than one node.

rows.label: Licence of the free broker
values: BSL 1.1 since 5.9.0 (May 2025); Apache 2.0 core up to 5.8
Community Edition: Apache 2.0; HiveMQ Platform is proprietary

rows.label: Clustering
values: Core and replicant nodes; needs a commercial licence (the free licence is single-node)
Masterless cluster in the paid Platform and Cloud; Community Edition is single-node
None in the open-source broker, only bridges between brokers; Cedalo’s commercial Pro Mosquitto adds clustering

rows.label: Other transports
values: WebSockets, MQTT over QUIC; MQTT-SN, CoAP, LwM2M gateways

rows.label: Data integration
values: Enterprise extensions (Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub, PostgreSQL, MongoDB)

sections.title: EMQX licences by version
sections.intro: Check which version you run: the licence changed twice in four years.

items.name: 1.0 to 4.x
items.text: The repository moved from MPL 1.1 (2012) to MIT (2014) to Apache 2.0 in February 2016, two months before emqttd 1.0.

items.name: 5.0 to 5.8
items.text: The core stayed Apache 2.0, but EMQX Enterprise code in the same repository, such as the Kafka connector, was under BSL 1.1. The 5.8 line got patches until 5.8.9 in December 2025.

items.name: 5.9.0 and later
items.text: One edition for everything. Free for non-production and single-node production, not as a hosted or embedded offering; education and non-profit use is free. Each version converts to Apache 2.0 four years after it is published, so 5.9.0 (May 2025) converts in 2029.

story: EMQX began in December 2012 as emqttd, an open-source MQTT broker written in Erlang; its 2014 licence file names Feng Lee as the copyright holder. After two years and more than fifty iterations, emqttd 1.0 shipped in April 2016 with full MQTT 3.1.1 support, clustering between broker nodes and a claim of 1 million connections on a single server.

EMQ, the company behind it, was founded in 2017 and is now based in Menlo Park, California, with offices including Hangzhou and Stockholm. Renamed EMQ X, the broker’s 3.0 release in December 2018 was its first to support MQTT 5.0. EMQX 5.0, in June 2022, added Mria: core nodes hold the shared tables and replicant nodes copy them asynchronously. EMQ reported 100 million MQTT clients on a 23-node cluster.

The licence followed the business. Version 5.0 put enterprise features under the Business Source License, and in May 2025 EMQX 5.9 merged the open-source and enterprise editions into one BSL 1.1 product. CEO Feng Lee said the change meant “accelerating our investment in MQTT and AI”.

choices.why: Erlang’s built-in distribution joins broker nodes into a cluster: each node is named `name@host`, nodes authenticate with a shared cookie and pass messages over TCP.

In a full-mesh cluster every node talks to every other. Mria lets replicants apply routing changes asynchronously, which cuts that network overhead and lets them scale up and down without affecting consistency.

choices.choice: A SQL rule engine inside the broker
choices.why: Filtering, transforming and routing messages in the broker, with no custom code, means device data can reach Kafka or a database without a separate bridge service to write and run.
EMQ wanted to keep the code public while funding development. BSL 1.1 lets anyone read and run it, limits production to a single node, and turns each version into Apache 2.0 after four years.
